04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The notation “manual approval” had seemed tantalising when Fiona Bell first reported it, but Emma knew that an unexplained label acquired meaning only when placed within the system that produced it. Fiona's next attachment provided part of that system: an extract from the Glenarraidh Education Trust's 2011 accounting guidance.

The document distinguished the initiation of an exceptional-payment request from its authorisation. An administrator could flag a case; a person exercising delegated authority was then expected to approve or refuse the proposed action. Separate dates and reference identifiers were to be recorded. No individual officer was named in the extract, and nothing in it established that staff had complied consistently.

Sarah read Emma's summary and asked whether two signatures were compulsory.

“Two recorded functions,” Emma replied. “That's what the guidance describes. It doesn't tell us whether approval was handwritten, entered in a system or documented on another sheet.”

The distinction mattered. Treating a procedural requirement as proof of its implementation was precisely the error Emma had tried to avoid with the selection notices and appeal rules. The absence of a legible name on a preliminary copy, meanwhile, did not prove that the original lacked an authorisation.

Fiona confirmed that the records team had observed manual-approval notations in some entries. However, adjacent fields were difficult to decipher, and the surviving pages had not been reconciled with subsequent accounting or banking evidence. The team was preparing clearer images before making any claim about quantities, signatories or outcomes.

Emma considered whether Helen Ward's cousin could help. The family possessed a redacted selection notice but no verified transfer record, and there was no documentary bridge to these accounting exceptions. Helen later relayed that her cousin permitted general enquiries about procedure but declined to disclose more personal banking material. Emma accepted that decision without trying to infer that withheld information concealed anything significant.

She revised her working model yet again. Requested did not mean authorised. Authorised did not mean transferred. Even a transfer recorded by the trust might not demonstrate receipt by the intended beneficiary. A returned transfer, a later correction or a change in course arrangements could explain divergent totals without implying impropriety. Each proposition demanded an appropriate source.

Then Fiona mentioned an unexamined inventory item headed “Delegated authority — September 2011”. It might describe the limits attached to particular posts, identify individuals who could authorise exceptional expenditure, or merely reproduce generic governance language. Fiona was unwilling to speculate before reading it.

The timing caught Emma's attention. A September document could be relevant to the period of the original selection announcement and Claire's disappearance. Yet a document bearing that month was not necessarily operative on the exact dates of either event. Its effective period would have to be established independently.

The anonymous caller's instruction—ask who approved the payments—now had an intelligible documentary direction. But the caller remained unidentified, and the guide did not corroborate any allegation of misconduct. It simply showed that authorisation and payment were administratively distinguishable.

Emma drafted a precise request to Fiona: could the records team identify the document's date, scope and named or role-based authority, while excluding students' personal details? She sent it without mentioning the caller.

For once, a potentially revealing clue was also a test of her patience. She would have to discover who could approve a payment before claiming to know who did.
